title: Leading Architecture Reviews and Assurance
objectives: Run effective architecture reviews that improve quality and build trust
Conduct peer reviews, design crits, and formal assurance with equal skill
Apply the Digital Assurance Playbook's principles to your review practice
Provide challenge that is honest, constructive, and actionable
Prepare teams for GDS service assessments from an architecture perspective
whyThisMatters:
Architecture reviews are the mechanism through which governance delivers value. A well-run review catches problems early, identifies opportunities, and builds the reviewing team's confidence that their architecture is sound. A poorly-run review damages trust, wastes time, and either fails to catch real problems or creates false confidence.

As a senior architect, you will both lead reviews and be reviewed. You will conduct peer reviews of colleagues' work, run formal design authority sessions, support teams preparing for GDS service assessments, and provide assurance for programmes across your department. Each context requires a different style — the challenge you offer in an informal peer review differs from the challenge you offer in a formal assurance role.

The Digital Assurance Playbook makes this even more important. With central spend controls removed, departmental assurance carries greater weight. The quality of your reviews directly affects whether your department catches problems before they become expensive or embarrassing. GDS will still support with high-risk and complex initiatives, but for most delivery, your organisation's architecture review capability is the primary quality assurance mechanism.

content.heading: Types of Architecture Review
content.body:
Architecture reviews exist on a spectrum from informal to formal, and the approach should match the context.

Peer Review is the most informal and frequent form. One architect reviews another's work — an ADR, a solution design, an integration approach. It happens daily in mature architecture teams. The tone is collaborative: 'have you considered...' rather than 'this is wrong.' Peer review works best when it is reciprocal and low-ceremony — a Slack message with a link, a 30-minute call to talk through an approach, a comment on a shared document.

Design Crit (or Architecture Crit) is a structured session where a team presents their architecture to a group of architects for challenge and feedback. It is more formal than peer review but less formal than governance. The presenting team walks through their design, the reviewers ask questions and offer alternatives, and the outcome is a set of recommendations (not directives). Design crits work well as a weekly or fortnightly practice within an architecture community.

Design Authority Review is a formal governance mechanism. A team submits a decision or design for approval by a panel with delegated authority. The outcome is a formal decision: approved, approved with conditions, or returned for rework. The documentation requirements are higher, and the review is recorded.

Formal Assurance is the most structured form. It follows a defined framework, typically aligned to the Technology Code of Practice and Service Standard, and produces a written assessment of confidence and risk. Under the Digital Assurance Playbook, this is what organisational assurance teams provide — and what GDS provides for high-risk initiatives.

Service Assessment is the GDS-led peer review that evaluates whether a digital service meets the Service Standard at each delivery phase. The assessment panel includes a lead assessor, user researcher, designer, technical lead, and sometimes a performance analyst. Assessments typically last about four hours. As an architect, you may both prepare teams for assessment and serve as a technical assessor yourself.

content.heading: The Reviewer's Mindset
content.body:
The most important skill in architecture review is not technical knowledge. It is the ability to ask questions that reveal problems without creating defensiveness. This is a mindset, not a technique.

Good reviewers start from curiosity, not judgement. They assume the team made reasonable decisions given their context, and seek to understand that context before challenging. 'Help me understand why you chose this approach' opens a productive conversation. 'Why on earth would you do it this way' closes it.

Good reviewers distinguish between preferences and problems. 'I would have done it differently' is not a review finding. 'This approach creates a single point of failure that will cause data loss during a region outage' is a review finding. Reserve your challenge for things that genuinely affect the quality, security, maintainability, or fitness for purpose of the solution.

Good reviewers are specific and actionable. 'The security model needs work' is unhelpful. 'The API gateway does not validate JWT signatures, which means any well-formed token will be accepted regardless of source — consider adding signature validation against the JWKS endpoint' is actionable.

Good reviewers acknowledge what is done well. Reviews that only identify problems create a punitive atmosphere. Noting what the team has done well — a clean separation of concerns, a thoughtful approach to data residency, a proportionate security model — builds trust and motivation.

Good reviewers calibrate challenge to maturity. A team in discovery exploring options needs different review from a team in late beta about to go live. Early-stage review should be expansive ('have you considered...'), late-stage review should be focused ('does this meet the non-functional requirements you defined?').

Good reviewers remember the power dynamic. When a senior architect reviews a junior team's work, there is an inherent power imbalance. What you intend as a suggestion may be received as a directive. Be explicit about which comments are blocking concerns and which are optional suggestions.

content.heading: Structuring an Effective Review Session
content.body:
A review session that rambles for two hours without reaching conclusions wastes everyone's time. Structure creates focus.

Before the session: define what is being reviewed and what questions the review should answer. Circulate materials in advance — at minimum, an architecture overview and the specific decisions or areas requiring review input. Reviewers who have not read the materials should not attend. Define the scope explicitly: 'We are reviewing the integration architecture for this service. We are not reviewing the front-end design or the data model today.'

Opening (5 minutes): The presenting team states what they are seeking from the review. This might be 'We want confidence that our security model is appropriate for OFFICIAL data' or 'We are choosing between two integration patterns and want advice on which to adopt.' Framing the review as a question the team needs answered — rather than as an exam — sets the right tone.

Presentation (15-20 minutes): The team walks through their architecture, focusing on the areas identified for review. Good presentations use diagrams, show the key decisions already made, and are honest about uncertainties and trade-offs. They do not present a polished sales pitch — they present the real state of the architecture, including the rough edges.

Clarification questions (10 minutes): Reviewers ask questions to ensure they understand the design before challenging it. These are questions like 'How does authentication work between these two components?' or 'What happens if this service is unavailable?' — not challenges disguised as questions.

Challenge and discussion (20-30 minutes): Reviewers offer challenges, alternatives, and concerns. The chair manages this to ensure all reviewers contribute and that the discussion does not get stuck on a single point. Challenges should be recorded in real time — not trusted to memory.

Summary and actions (5-10 minutes): The chair summarises the key findings, distinguishing between blocking concerns (must be addressed), recommendations (should be addressed), and observations (for consideration). Each action has an owner and a timeline. The presenting team confirms they understand and accept the actions.

After the session: Write up findings within 24 hours while they are fresh. Share with the presenting team and record in the governance repository. Follow up on actions at the next appropriate checkpoint.

content.heading: What to Look For: The Architecture Review Checklist
content.body:
While every review is contextual, certain categories of concern apply to most government service architectures. This is not an exhaustive checklist but a set of lenses to apply.

Fitness for purpose: Does the architecture actually solve the problem it claims to solve? Does it support the user journeys? Does it handle the expected volumes? Does it meet the non-functional requirements? It is surprisingly common for architectures to be technically elegant but not actually fit for the stated purpose.

Security and data protection: Is the security model appropriate for the data classification? Are there authentication and authorisation mechanisms at every trust boundary? Has the team engaged with Secure by Design principles? Is personal data handled in compliance with UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018? Are there data residency requirements and are they met?

Resilience and operability: What happens when components fail? Is there a single point of failure? How is the service monitored? What is the recovery approach? Has the team designed for the support model — will operations teams have the tools they need?

Scalability and performance: Can the architecture handle the expected load? What about peak load? What about growth over time? Are there capacity constraints that will become bottlenecks? Has the team done any performance modelling or testing?

Maintainability and evolvability: Can the architecture be changed when requirements change? Are components loosely coupled? Are interfaces well-defined? Will a new team be able to understand and modify this architecture without the original designers?

Standards alignment: Does the architecture align with the Technology Code of Practice? Does it support the Service Standard? Does it follow departmental architecture principles and patterns? If it deviates, is the deviation justified and documented?

Reuse and duplication: Has the team checked for existing solutions before building new ones? Are they using shared government platforms (GOV.UK One Login, GOV.UK Notify, GOV.UK Pay) where appropriate? Are they aware of similar services in other departments?

Cost proportionality: Is the architecture proportionate to the problem? Is there unnecessary complexity or over-engineering? Are the cost projections realistic given the technology choices?

content.heading: Assurance Under the Digital Assurance Playbook
content.body:
The Digital Assurance Playbook defines a specific framework for how assurance works post-April 2026. As a senior architect, you need to understand this framework because you will likely play a role in your organisation's assurance function.

Assurance operates on at least three levels. The first line is the operational management team that owns and manages risk — this is the delivery team and their architect. The second line is senior management, independent of operational management, using specialist expertise — this is your design authority or architecture review function. The third line is independent bodies providing an objective view — this might be internal audit, GDS central assurance, or external reviewers.

The Playbook identifies specific areas that assurance should test. Meeting outcomes — are the initiative's objectives clearly defined and realistic? Strategic alignment — does the initiative align with organisational and government digital strategy? Avoiding duplication — has duplicative delivery been avoided? Standards alignment — is the initiative following government digital standards? Service Manual compliance — for new services, is the team following Service Manual principles? Cyber security — is the team following Secure by Design? Legacy debt — will the initiative tackle existing debt or avoid creating new debt? Cloud First — are cloud delivery principles being followed? Data use — are data regulations being followed? AI use — for AI initiatives, are the AI Playbook principles being followed? ATRS compliance — for algorithmic tools, is the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard being met? Accessibility — are accessibility regulations and standards being met?

As an architect conducting assurance, you use these areas as a framework but apply them proportionately. A small internal tool does not need the same depth of assurance as a citizen-facing service processing millions of transactions. The Playbook explicitly states that assurance should be proportionate to risk and value.

Your assurance output should be clear and actionable: what confidence level do you have (high, medium, low) that the initiative will succeed, what are the key risks, and what specific actions would increase confidence? Avoid vague findings like 'security needs improvement.' Instead: 'The service stores personal data but has no documented threat model. Recommend the team completes a threat modelling exercise with security before beta assessment.'

content.heading: Preparing Teams for GDS Service Assessments
content.body:
GDS service assessments are structured peer-led reviews where an independent panel evaluates whether a digital service meets the Service Standard. The panel typically includes a lead assessor, user researcher, designer, technical lead, and sometimes a performance analyst. Assessments last about four hours: the team presents and demonstrates their service, then assessors ask questions.

As the architect supporting a team through assessment, your preparation role includes:

Ensuring the architecture supports the full Service Standard, not just the technology points. The standard covers user needs, accessibility, team capability, iteration, and operational concerns — all of which have architecture implications. A beautiful technical architecture that does not support user needs or accessibility will fail assessment.

Preparing the team to explain their architecture decisions clearly. Assessors ask 'why' questions: why did you choose this technology? Why this hosting model? Why this integration pattern? Teams that cannot articulate the reasoning behind their decisions — even if the decisions are sound — struggle at assessment. ADRs are excellent preparation material.

Identifying and addressing gaps before assessment. Conduct a mock assessment using the Service Standard points. Common gaps for architecture: missing non-functional requirements, no evidence of performance testing, no operational readiness evidence, accessibility not considered at the architecture level, no clear approach to data protection.

Coaching the team on what assessors look for from a technical perspective. Assessors want to see: evidence of good decision-making (options considered, trade-offs articulated), alignment with the Technology Code of Practice, appropriate use of shared platforms, security by design, and a realistic understanding of operational requirements. They do not want to see: technology choices made without rationale, monolithic architectures without justification, security as an afterthought, or over-engineering for the problem at hand.

Being available during the assessment. The technical assessor will ask detailed questions about architecture. The team's architect should be present to answer these — not to dominate the conversation, but to provide the depth that developers or product owners may not be able to.

content.heading: Delivering Difficult Messages
content.body:
The hardest part of architecture review is not identifying problems. It is communicating them in a way that leads to action rather than defensiveness. This is especially challenging when the review reveals fundamental issues — an architecture that will not scale, a security model that is inadequate, or a design that will create unsustainable technical debt.

Separate the work from the person. 'This architecture has a scalability constraint' is about the work. 'You designed this without thinking about scalability' is about the person. The first invites problem-solving. The second invites defensiveness.

Be direct but not brutal. Government culture sometimes conflates politeness with avoiding difficult conversations. This leads to reviews where concerns are hinted at but never stated clearly. The team leaves thinking everything is fine. Two months later, the problem materialises. Be direct: 'This will not handle the expected load. Here is why.' But be respectful: do not grandstand, do not use technical superiority to embarrass, and do not make it personal.

Offer solutions alongside problems. 'This will not scale' is a problem. 'This will not scale because the synchronous database writes create a bottleneck at 500 concurrent users. Consider an event-driven approach with eventual consistency for the non-critical paths' is a problem with a path forward. Not every problem needs a fully specified solution from the reviewer, but giving direction shows that the problem is solvable.

Distinguish severity levels explicitly. Not all review findings are equal. Make it clear which findings are blocking (must be resolved before proceeding), which are significant (should be resolved but can be tracked), and which are advisory (worth considering but not required). Teams need to know where to focus their effort.

Follow up. A review that identifies problems but never checks whether they were addressed is incomplete. Build follow-up into your review process — whether that is a re-review session, a check at the next governance meeting, or a simple confirmation that actions have been completed.

Know when to escalate. If a review identifies a serious problem — a security vulnerability, a design that cannot meet legal requirements, an architecture that will fail in production — and the team or programme chooses not to address it, you have a duty to escalate. This is uncomfortable but essential. Document your concern, state the risk clearly, and escalate to the appropriate level of governance. This is what the three lines of assurance model is designed for.

content.heading: Building a Review Culture
content.body:
Individual reviews improve individual architectures. A review culture improves the entire organisation's architecture capability over time.

A healthy review culture has several characteristics. Reviews are expected, not exceptional — every significant architecture decision gets reviewed as a matter of course, not because someone raised a concern. Reviews are reciprocal — senior architects submit their work for review by peers, not just junior teams submitting to seniors. Reviews are timely — they happen early enough to influence direction, not so late that change is prohibitively expensive. Reviews are constructive — the default assumption is that the team is trying to do good work and the review helps them do it better.

Building this culture requires deliberate action. Start with peer review among the architecture community — architects reviewing each other's ADRs and designs in a low-stakes, collaborative format. This builds the muscle of giving and receiving feedback before it is applied in higher-stakes governance contexts.

Run regular design crits where teams present work-in-progress to the architecture community. Make attendance voluntary and the atmosphere supportive. Share patterns and approaches that emerge — 'Team A solved a similar problem this way' — to build collective knowledge.

Celebrate good architecture publicly. When a review identifies something well-done — an elegant integration pattern, a thoughtful approach to accessibility, a security model that is both robust and usable — share it as an example for others. Architecture communities of practice are excellent venues for this.

The cross-government architecture community provides models for this. The technical architecture community has regular cross-government lunches and architecture drinks. The Government Data Architecture Community (GDAC) brings together data architects across central and local government. These communities normalise the practice of sharing work, receiving feedback, and learning from others.

workedExample.title: Architecture Review of a Cross-Government Data Sharing Service
workedExample.context: The Government Digital Service is developing a new cross-government data sharing capability as part of the Roadmap for Modern Digital Government. The service will allow departments to share reference data about citizens (with appropriate legal gateways and data protection safeguards) to avoid asking citizens for the same information multiple times. The alpha phase has been completed and the team is preparing for beta assessment. You have been asked to conduct a formal architecture review as the departmental representative before the team proceeds to the cross-government service assessment.
workedExample.approach:
The architect structures the review around the key areas from the Digital Assurance Playbook and the Service Standard.

Pre-review preparation (2 days): The architect requests and reviews the solution architecture document, the data protection impact assessment, the threat model, the ADRs recorded during alpha, and the technical spike outcomes. They note initial questions and areas of concern.

Review session (3 hours):

The team presents: the user need (departments currently re-ask citizens for data they have already provided to government), the data sharing model (a federated approach where data remains in source systems but is queryable through a standard API), the security model (mutual TLS between departments, OAuth2 for service-to-service authorisation, audit logging of all queries), and the data governance model (legal gateways for each data share, automated data minimisation, retention policies enforced at the API layer).

The architect's challenge focuses on five areas:

1. Scalability: The alpha tested with 3 departments and 50,000 queries per day. Beta will include 8 departments and an estimated 2 million queries per day. Has the team load-tested at beta volumes? (Finding: they have not. Recommendation: load testing before beta go-live.)

2. Failure modes: What happens when a source department's system is unavailable? The current design returns an error to the consuming department. (Finding: no graceful degradation. Recommendation: implement a caching layer for reference data with defined staleness tolerances per data type.)

3. Data protection: The DPIA covers the current 3-department scope. Will it be updated for the expanded 8-department scope? Each new department introduces new legal gateways and new data types. (Finding: DPIA update is planned but not yet started. Recommendation: DPIA must be updated and signed off before new departments are onboarded.)

4. Operational model: Who operates this service when it is live? It is currently maintained by the GDS development team, but long-term ownership is unclear. (Finding: no defined operational model. Recommendation: agree the long-term ownership and support model before live assessment.)

5. Standards alignment: The API follows the GDS API technical and data standards. The service uses GOV.UK One Login for administrator access. The architecture records are maintained as ADRs in the cross-government template. (Finding: good alignment. No concerns.)
workedExample.outcome: The review produces a formal assessment with confidence level 'Medium' — the architecture is fundamentally sound but has gaps in scalability evidence, operational readiness, and data protection coverage for the expanded scope. Three blocking actions (load testing, DPIA update, operational model) and two recommendations (caching layer, monitoring enhancement) are recorded. The team addresses all blocking actions within four weeks and proceeds to beta assessment, where they pass with minor recommendations.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The review's value was not in finding fundamental design flaws — the architecture was well-designed. The value was in identifying gaps that would have caused problems later: a service that had not been load-tested at realistic volumes, a data protection assessment that was out of date, and an operational model that was undefined. These are exactly the kinds of issues that cause problems in live service and that assessors challenge at beta assessment. By catching them in departmental review, the team had time to address them before facing external scrutiny.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Architecture Review That Nobody Listened To
civilServiceScenario.background: Six months ago, you conducted an architecture review of a new citizen-facing service at your department. The review identified a significant concern: the service's dependency on a third-party API with no SLA, no fallback mechanism, and no caching. You recorded this as a blocking concern and recommended the team implement a circuit breaker pattern with a cached fallback. The programme manager acknowledged the finding but stated that addressing it would delay the launch by three weeks, which was unacceptable due to a ministerial commitment. The finding was recorded as 'accepted risk.' The service launched on time. Yesterday, the third-party API went down for six hours. The service was completely unavailable. 50,000 citizens could not complete their applications. The outage made regional news. The permanent secretary is asking questions.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: The programme board has convened an emergency session. You have been asked to present: what happened, why it happened, what was known in advance, and what needs to change. You need to be honest about the review finding without being self-righteous or blaming the programme manager who overrode it.
constraints: Your review finding is documented and timestamped
The programme manager's decision to accept the risk is also documented
The permanent secretary was not aware of the accepted risk — it was not escalated
The third-party API provider has no contractual obligation for availability
The ministerial commitment that drove the launch date was real and politically important
The same programme manager is still responsible for the service and is under significant pressure
The operational team had no runbook for this failure scenario
The service has no monitoring for the third-party API — the outage was discovered when users complained
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect who conducted the original review and identified the risk. You have been asked to present the technical analysis to the emergency programme board and recommend a path forward.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This scenario tests how you handle the aftermath of a review finding being overridden. The temptation is to say 'I told you so.' Resist it. The goal is not to assign blame but to fix the problem and prevent recurrence.

Your presentation should: state the facts neutrally (the review identified this risk, it was accepted, the accepted risk materialised), explain the technical cause clearly (no fallback mechanism, no monitoring, no runbook), propose immediate remediation (implement the circuit breaker and cached fallback — the same recommendation from six months ago), and recommend governance improvements (risks of this severity should have been escalated beyond the programme, accepted risks should be reviewed at a defined cadence, critical dependencies should be monitored regardless of whether the risk is accepted).

The governance lesson is about escalation and risk visibility. The review process worked — it identified the risk. The governance process failed — it allowed a significant risk to be accepted without appropriate visibility to senior leadership. The fix is not to make the architecture review more powerful, but to ensure that accepted risks above a certain severity are visible to those accountable for the service.

practiceArtefact.description: You have just completed an architecture review of a new digital service that allows UK businesses to submit environmental compliance data to DESNZ. The service is in late beta and approaching its live assessment. Produce a formal review report that covers: the scope of your review, key findings (both positive and concerning), an overall confidence assessment, and specific actionable recommendations.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Structure your report for two audiences: the delivery team (who need specific, actionable findings) and senior leadership (who need a summary confidence level and key risks). Use a traffic-light system for confidence: Green (high confidence, proceed), Amber (medium confidence, address findings before proceeding), Red (low confidence, significant rework required). For each finding, state what you observed, why it matters, and what action you recommend. Be specific enough that the team can act on your findings without needing another meeting to understand them.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Architecture Review Report — Environmental Compliance Reporting Service**

Date: [Date] | Reviewer: [Name] | Phase: Late Beta (pre-live assessment)

**Executive Summary:**
Overall confidence: AMBER. The architecture is fundamentally sound and well-aligned with government standards. Three findings require attention before live assessment: incomplete disaster recovery testing, missing accessibility at the document upload component, and undefined data retention implementation.

**Scope:**
Reviewed: Solution architecture, security model, operational readiness, non-functional requirements coverage, standards alignment.
Not reviewed: Code quality, detailed database design, front-end implementation detail.

**Positive Findings:**
- Clean separation between the submission service and the assessment workflow — enables independent scaling and deployment
- Good use of GOV.UK Notify for all user communications — consistent and accessible
- Security model appropriate for OFFICIAL data with well-defined trust boundaries
- ADRs well-maintained with clear rationale — will support assessment panel questions
- API design follows GDS API technical and data standards

**Findings Requiring Action:**

1. BLOCKING — Disaster Recovery Not Tested
Observation: The DR plan documents recovery to a secondary region with an RTO of 4 hours. However, this has never been tested. The secondary region has the infrastructure deployed but no evidence it can accept production traffic.
Why it matters: The Service Standard requires evidence that the service can recover from failure. Assessors will ask about DR testing.
Recommendation: Conduct a full DR failover test before live assessment. Document the results and any issues discovered.

2. BLOCKING — Document Upload Accessibility Gap
Observation: The document upload component does not provide adequate feedback to screen reader users when upload fails. Error messages are visual only.
Why it matters: The Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations require WCAG 2.2 AA compliance. This component fails WCAG 4.1.3 (Status Messages).
Recommendation: Implement ARIA live regions for upload status and error messages. Retest with screen reader.

3. SIGNIFICANT — Data Retention Not Implemented
Observation: The data retention policy states records are deleted after 7 years. However, no automated deletion mechanism exists. The team plans to implement it 'later.'
Why it matters: Without automated retention, data will accumulate indefinitely. This creates GDPR risk and storage cost growth. Assessors may challenge the gap between stated policy and implementation.
Recommendation: Implement automated retention before live. If not feasible, implement monitoring that alerts when records approach retention age, with a defined plan for full automation within 6 months.

4. ADVISORY — Monitoring Coverage
Observation: Application-level monitoring is comprehensive, but there is no synthetic monitoring (proactive checks from the user's perspective).
Why it matters: Without synthetic monitoring, outages are detected when users report them rather than proactively.
Recommendation: Implement synthetic monitoring for the critical user journeys (submit report, check status).

reflectiveQuestions: Think about the last architecture review you conducted or received. Was the feedback specific and actionable, or vague and unhelpful? What made the difference?
How do you balance being honest about problems with maintaining a constructive relationship with the delivery team? Can you think of a time you got this balance wrong?
Has a review finding you raised ever been overridden by a programme decision? How did you handle it? Would you handle it differently now?
What is the most valuable piece of feedback you have ever received in an architecture review? What made it valuable — the content, the delivery, or the timing?
How would you assess your organisation's review culture? Is it collaborative and constructive, or performative and adversarial? What one thing could you do to improve it?

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most important skill for conducting effective architecture reviews?
options: Deep technical knowledge in all technology domains
The ability to ask questions that reveal problems without creating defensiveness
Experience of building large-scale distributed systems
Familiarity with every government standard and framework
knowledgeCheck.explanation: While technical knowledge is necessary, the most important skill is the ability to ask questions that reveal problems constructively. A reviewer who identifies problems but creates defensiveness will not influence change. The mindset of curiosity over judgement, combined with specific and actionable feedback, is what makes reviews effective.

knowledgeCheck.question: Under the Digital Assurance Playbook, at how many levels should assurance typically operate?
options: One — the central GDS assurance team
Two — departmental and central
At least three — operational management, independent senior management, and independent bodies
Five — team, programme, department, function, and Treasury
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Digital Assurance Playbook states that assurance should typically be on at least three separate levels: by the operational management team that owns risk, by senior management independent of operations using specialist expertise, and by independent bodies providing an objective view on governance and risk management effectiveness.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the key difference between a Design Crit and a Design Authority Review?
options: Design Crits are for junior staff while Design Authority Reviews are for seniors
Design Crits produce recommendations while Design Authority Reviews produce formal decisions
Design Crits are about user interface and Design Authority Reviews are about backend architecture
There is no meaningful difference between them
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A Design Crit is a structured feedback session where reviewers offer recommendations — the presenting team decides what to act on. A Design Authority Review is a formal governance mechanism where the panel has delegated authority to approve, conditionally approve, or return decisions for rework. The outcome is a binding governance decision, not just advice.

knowledgeCheck.question: When preparing a team for a GDS service assessment, what do technical assessors primarily look for?
options: The most advanced and modern technology stack available
Evidence of good decision-making with options considered and trade-offs articulated
A perfect architecture with no compromises or technical debt
Compliance with a specific architecture framework like TOGAF
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Assessors want to see evidence of thoughtful decision-making: options considered, trade-offs articulated, alignment with the Technology Code of Practice, appropriate use of shared platforms, and realistic understanding of operational requirements. They are not looking for perfection or specific frameworks — they are looking for a team that understands why their architecture is the way it is.

knowledgeCheck.question: What should you do if an architecture review identifies a serious risk that the programme chooses not to address?
options: Accept the decision silently since the programme has authority over delivery
Refuse to approve any further architecture work until the risk is addressed
Document the risk, ensure it is visible to those accountable, and escalate if severity warrants it
Raise it repeatedly at every meeting until the team agrees to fix it
knowledgeCheck.explanation: When a serious risk is accepted by a programme, the architect's responsibility is to ensure it is documented, visible to those accountable for the service, and escalated through appropriate governance if the severity warrants senior attention. Simply accepting silently creates a governance gap. Refusing to work or raising it repeatedly is counterproductive.
